what_it_does: Matrix multiplication — multiplying two large grids of numbers together — is the core operation inside almost every AI model. The most common hardware for it is a systolic array: a grid of tiny multiplier units that pass numbers from neighbor to neighbor in a wave-like rhythm, which works very efficiently when the matrices are dense (mostly non-zero numbers). Real AI workloads increasingly have sparse matrices — grids where most values are zero and can be skipped to save work — but adding sparsity-handling circuits to a systolic array usually makes it bigger and more power-hungry, hurting the common dense case. DenSparSA adds lightweight extra circuits to a standard systolic array that kick in only when the data is sparse; for dense workloads those circuits are electrically disabled (gated off) so they cost nothing. The design reportedly handles matrices that are sparse on one side (one of the two input grids) or on both sides, without penalizing the dense case.
